title: Illness: feeling under the weather
subtitle: off-colour, come down with, on the mend
summary: Use the everyday idioms English speakers really use for minor illness - from feeling under the weather and coming down with flu to being back on your feet again.

lesson.heading: Feeling unwell: four informal idioms
lesson.text: These all mean 'not well, but not seriously ill'. To look **off-colour** is to look pale and unwell. To feel **out of sorts** is to feel slightly unwell and slightly low. To feel **under the weather** is the commonest of all - mildly ill, enough to stay at home. And **poorly** is a gentle, rather homely word for ill, often used of children.

examples.text: *A:* You look a bit **off-colour** today. Are you all right? *B:* I'm just feeling a bit **out of sorts**, it's nothing to worry about.
I was feeling a bit **under the weather**, so I stayed at home yesterday.
Katy's been feeling **poorly** for a while.

lesson.note: Say under the weather, not ~~out of the weather~~, and out of sorts, not ~~off the sorts~~.

lesson.heading: Catching things and fighting them off
lesson.text: To **fight off** an illness is to try to get rid of it. To **go down with** something is to catch it, usually a non-serious illness - but we normally say **come down with** when talking about ourselves. For longer-term problems we use **suffer from**.

examples.text: I'm **fighting off** a cold at the moment.
Rani isn't in today; she's **gone down with** flu.
I've **come down with** a dreadful cold.
Harry **suffers from** hay fever and sneezes a lot if he's near grass or flowers.

lesson.heading: hurt and ache

left.label: hurt
left.text: Gives pain caused by an injury. As a noun, hurt means emotional pain.
examples: My arm **hurts** where I banged it against the car door.
The break-up of their relationship caused them both deep **hurt**.

right.label: ache
right.text: A persistent low-level pain. A physical pain can be a dull, nagging or throbbing **ache**, and it forms compounds: backache, headache, toothache.
examples: My back **aches** after all that digging yesterday.
Maria has **backache** after carrying that heavy suitcase.

lesson.note: Two fixed expressions, always in this order: the usual aches and pains (not ~~pains and aches~~) for minor problems, and cuts and bruises (not ~~bruises and cuts~~) for minor injuries.

lesson.heading: Kinds of physical discomfort
rows: a sudden, burning pain - My hand's been stinging ever since I touched that plant.
beat with pain - My head is throbbing.
pain and difficulty in moving your neck round
injure it by turning it suddenly
a feeling that you are spinning round and can't balance
with a high temperature or fever
shaking slightly, usually because of a fever
feeling that you want to vomit
blocked - informal, used of the nose

lesson.heading: Sleepless nights and other complaints
lesson.text: Notice how these words work in real sentences. A **sleepless night** is one without much sleep, and if your head is **throbbing** it is beating with pain, so a painkiller is the answer.

examples.text: I've had a lot of **sleepless nights** recently.
She **tripped** on the uneven pavement and **twisted her ankle**.
I had a terrible **nauseous** feeling after taking the medicine, but it passed.
My nose is all **bunged up** today with this horrible cold.

lesson.heading: Getting better
lesson.text: To **get over** an illness is to recover from it, usually a minor one. **Recover from** is used for more serious illnesses. To be **on the mend** is to be getting better and heading back towards normal. To be **over the worst** is to be past the most difficult period, though still quite ill. To be **back on your feet again** is to be fully healthy once more.

examples.text: I had a virus last week, but I **got over** it quite quickly.
Dan felt terrible last week, but he's **on the mend** now.
It's taking Hania some time to recover, but she's **over the worst** now.
She'll be **back on her feet again** soon.

lesson.text: Over the worst still means quite ill; on the mend means nearly normal; back on your feet means completely better.

exercises.prompt: Match each idiom with its meaning.

pairs.right: try to get rid of it

exercises.prompt: I feel a bit under the ___ today, but I'm sure I'll be fine tomorrow.
exercises.explanation: Under the weather means slightly unwell - never ~~out of the weather~~.

exercises.prompt: Nadja, I won't be in today, I've ___ with a cold.
exercises.explanation: We usually say come down with, not go down with, when talking about ourselves.

exercises.prompt: I'm trying to ___ the flu, but nothing seems to help.
exercises.explanation: To fight off an illness is to try to get rid of it.

exercises.prompt: Hello, Dan, good to see you back on your ___ again.
exercises.explanation: To be back on your feet again is to be completely well once more.

exercises.prompt: I'm OK. I'm over the ___ now. I still feel bad, but I should be out of hospital within a week.
exercises.explanation: Over the worst suggests you are improving but still quite ill.

exercises.prompt: I used to ___ a dust allergy, but I don't think I do any more.
exercises.explanation: You suffer from a long-term problem - suffer from, never ~~suffer of~~.

exercises.prompt: My nose was all ___ up, so I got a spray from the chemist.
exercises.explanation: Bunged up is an informal way of saying blocked, used about the nose.

exercises.prompt: I felt as if my head was spinning, so I went and lay down. I was very ___ .
exercises.explanation: Dizzy is the feeling that you are spinning round and cannot balance.

exercises.prompt: I got a ___ neck from driving for a long time in an awkward position.
exercises.explanation: A stiff neck gives you pain and difficulty in moving your neck round.

exercises.prompt: 'The smell of paint always made her feel that she wanted to vomit.' Which word says this best?
exercises.explanation: Nauseous is the feeling that you want to vomit.

exercises.statement: Mum's feeling fine, apart from the usual pains and aches.
exercises.explanation: The fixed expression is the usual aches and pains, in that order. The same goes for cuts and bruises.

exercises.prompt: Does each expression describe health improving or health going wrong?

items.text: be back on your feet again
